prompt:

   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)

 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?

   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?

   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
   "tn1": Does it sell into a real secular trend (like AI, energy or robotics; ideally the infrastructure layer), as a company built for that trend rather than an old business retrofitting?
   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?
   "tn3": Is it outside the zones to avoid: small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups?
   "tn4": Of these three, does it pass at least two (and have a valid reason for any miss, such as infrastructure needing leverage or a clear path to profit): revenue grown for the past few years, profitable, more cash than debt?
   "tn5": Has free cash flow been positive, and cash exceeded debt, in each of the last 4 to 6 quarters?
   "tn6": Is revenue growing at 10% a year or more?
   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: AB InBev fails most Rule Breaker traits: it leads a mature, slow-growing beer industry rather than an emerging one. It does have top brands and strong price momentum over the past year (shares about +36%), but it is a Rule Maker-style incumbent, not a disruptor.
summaries.buffett: Buffett-style strengths are clear: simple products, world-leading brands (8 of the 10 most valuable beer brands) and $11.3B of FY2025 free cash flow. Against that, ROIC is modest because of $118B of goodwill, debt is heavy at 2.86x EBITDA, ten-year EPS is below 2015's $5.05, and the price (about 22x underlying earnings) offers little margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would like the brand moat and scale economics but dislike the debt load, the long record of value-destroying acquisition financing (SABMiller in 2016) and the slow-growth category. It is a good business at a fair-to-full price rather than a wonderful one at a fair price.
summaries.lynch: In Lynch's terms it is a stalwart that has been a partial turnaround since its 2020 dividend cut and deleveraging. At about 19x forward earnings with EPS growth expected near 18% for 2026 (much of it currency and lower interest), the PEG is roughly 1.2, so it is reasonably but not cheaply priced.
summaries.fisher: Fisher-style it scores well on sales organisation, brand building and cost control, and is developing new products (Beyond Beer +44% in 2Q26, Michelob Ultra Zero, BEES). It scores poorly on long-run sales growth potential and margin expansion at gross level.
summaries.graham: It passes Graham's size, dividend-record and earnings-continuity tests only partly, and fails on valuation: about 28x three-year average EPS and P/E × P/B near 46, a current ratio of 0.72, and EPS that has fallen over ten years.
summaries.thiel: AB InBev is not a Zero to One business: no proprietary technology, a mature market and growth by acquisition. Its durable distribution and brand position answers Thiel's durability and distribution questions well, but not the others.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable growth at reasonable prices with efficient operations; AB InBev offers efficiency (35.8% EBITDA margin, buybacks) and improving EPS, but its organic growth of about 2-6% and lack of a secular tailwind make it a weak fit for his growth focus.
summaries.druckenmiller: Momentum and earnings revisions are positive (shares at a 1-year high after six straight EPS beats, consensus FY2026 EPS growth about 18%), and a weaker dollar has helped reported results. But it is a slow-growth consumer staple, unlikely to be a large concentrated bet in his style.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith's quality tests are mixed: gross margin of 56% and high cash conversion pass, but return on capital is low because of acquisition goodwill, leverage is high, and growth is slow; Fundsmith-type investors have preferred spirits and soft drinks.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula, earnings yield (EBIT/EV about 6.9%) is middling and return on tangible capital is decent excluding goodwill, so it would rank as average rather than a standout cheap, high-return stock.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool: the business quality leg is solid (brands, scale), the management leg is decent (disciplined capital allocation under Doukeris), but the reinvestment leg is weak because the mature beer market offers few high-return reinvestment opportunities.
summaries.pabrai: Dhandho principles favor simple, durable businesses bought at a deep discount; AB InBev is simple and durable with low permanent-loss risk, but at roughly 22x underlying earnings and 6.8% FCF yield it is not the heads-I-win discount Pabrai seeks.
summaries.wood: AB InBev has no exposure to ARK's disruptive platforms (AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain, multiomics) beyond using data in its BEES app, so it fits Cathie Wood's framework poorly.
summaries.ackman: Ackman's criteria (simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative, dominant, with a catalyst) are partly met: brands are dominant and cash flow strong, while deleveraging and buybacks are catalysts. High debt and FX exposure reduce predictability.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's scale-economics-shared model fits only partly: AB InBev uses its scale mainly to raise margins and pay down debt rather than to cut prices for customers, so the flywheel favors shareholders over consumers.
summaries.valentine: Don Valentine sought huge, fast-growing markets created by technology shifts; a 150-year-old brewing business in a flat beer market is the opposite of what Sequoia looks for.
summaries.nash: AB InBev fails most of Nash's hard filters: debt far exceeds cash, revenue growth is below 10% and it sells into no secular trend, scoring about 60 of 130 on his categories. Its strengths are an operating margin above 25%, consistent earnings beats and a dominant brand portfolio.

momentum.evidence: The ADS closed at $82.59 on 16 Oct 2026, up about 36% from about $60.90 a year earlier and about 9% over six months, reaching a 1-year high after Q2 2026 results.

g4.evidence: CEO Michel Doukeris has a strong execution record, and the controlling Stichting AB InBev reference shareholder includes the Brazilian 3G founders' families (Lemann, Telles, Sicupira) alongside Altria as a large holder.

g6.evidence: Analysts mostly rate it a Buy with an average target of $95.26 (StockAnalysis, Oct 2026), so it is not widely called overvalued.

simple.evidence: It brews and sells beer through well-known brands; the business is easy for a generalist to understand.

b2.evidence: Revenue rose from $46.9B (2020) to $59.3B (2025) and normalized EBITDA margin to 35.8%, but EPS fell from $5.05 (2015) to $3.45 (2025) after the SABMiller deal and the 2020 pandemic.

integrity.evidence: Reporting is detailed and capital allocation has been disciplined since 2021 (deleveraging, $6B buyback), but the 2016 SABMiller deal overloaded the balance sheet, dividends were cut in 2018 and 2020, and control sits with a reference shareholder.

b6.evidence: Under Doukeris it has avoided large deals and focused on organic growth and debt reduction, but its history (InBev–Anheuser-Busch 2008, Grupo Modelo 2013, SABMiller 2016) is one of empire-building through mega-mergers.

roic.evidence: With $117.9B of goodwill and $73B of interest-bearing debt against $15.4B of FY2025 profit from operations, returns on total invested capital are only high single digits and rely on leverage.

fcf.evidence: FY2025 free cash flow (operating cash flow $14,883M minus net capex $3,552M) was $11,331M, above profit attributable of $6,837M.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings were used for acquisitions and debt repayment, yet EPS of $3.45 in 2025 is below $5.05 in 2015 and the share price is below its 2015-2016 levels.

safety.evidence: A conservative DCF on its 3-year average growth (0.9%) and FCF margin (17.6%) gives about $27 per share at 12% and $47 at 10%, well below the $82.59 price.

fairprice.evidence: At about 22x FY2025 underlying EPS of $3.73, 19x forward EPS of $4.40 and a 6.8% FCF yield, the price is fair for a dominant brewer but not cheap given slow growth.

mu5.evidence: Beer demand is stable and the brands are durable, but failure paths exist: high leverage, emerging-market currency shocks, consumer boycotts and a long-term shift away from alcohol.

reinvest.evidence: Net capex runs about $3.5-4.0B a year against $11.3B of free cash flow, with most cash going to debt reduction, dividends and buybacks because the mature beer market offers few high-return reinvestments.

ly2.evidence: It is a stalwart with a simple story: premium megabrands, price/mix gains, deleveraging and buybacks driving mid-to-high single-digit EBITDA and faster EPS growth.

ly3.evidence: Trailing P/E is about 24x (diluted EPS $3.39), above its EPS growth rate; MarketBeat lists a PEG of 1.19.

runway.evidence: Growth in Middle and South America, Africa, Beyond Beer and BEES Marketplace offer some runway, but consensus sees revenue CAGR of only about 5-6% to FY2028.

ly7.evidence: The company is reducing its share count through a $6B buyback ($1.9B completed by 24 July 2026), but no notable open-market insider buying was found.

ly8.evidence: It is one of the most widely covered consumer stocks, with about 26 analysts forecasting revenue.

fi2.evidence: Management launches new products as old ones mature (Michelob Ultra Zero, Cutwater, Nütrl, Beyond Beer revenue +44% in 2Q26), though most are line extensions.

fi3.evidence: It does not disclose material R&D spending; innovation results show mainly in marketing-driven brand launches rather than R&D output.

fi4.evidence: Its sales and marketing machine is world class: Corona grew 17% outside Mexico in 2Q26 and BEES processed $15.0B of GMV in 2Q26.

longterm.evidence: Investment in BEES, Beyond Beer and megabrand marketing shows long-term thinking, but the zero-based-budgeting culture prioritises near-term margins and cost cuts.

gr1.evidence: It is the world's largest brewer with $59.3B of FY2025 revenue and a market value of about $166B.

ni10.evidence: Profit attributable to shareholders was positive every year from 2016 to 2025 (e.g. $1,241M in 2016, $1,405M in 2020), but 2020 showed a $650M loss from continuing operations.

gr4.evidence: It has paid a dividend annually for more than 20 years, but cut it sharply in 2018 and 2020 (the FY2025 total was €1.15 per share versus $3.85 per share in 2016).

eps10.evidence: Basic EPS fell from $5.05 in 2015 to $3.45 in 2025.

gr6.evidence: The price is about 28x average diluted EPS for 2023-2025 ($2.95).

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 24x times P/B of about 1.9x gives roughly 46, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Beer brewing has no proprietary technology ten times better than rivals.

timing.evidence: Timing is helped by deleveraging and a weaker dollar boosting reported revenue (HY26 +11.5% reported), but beer category volumes are flat to declining.

th3.evidence: It grew by consolidating an already large global beer market through mega-acquisitions, not by dominating a small niche.

team.evidence: Management is highly capable and disciplined, but it is a professional, not founder-led, team.

th5.evidence: Its route-to-market and BEES digital platform reaching millions of retailers are a powerful distribution advantage.

durable.evidence: Brands like Budweiser (founded 1876), Corona and Stella Artois and its scale distribution are likely to hold their position for decades, even if the category grows slowly.

th7.evidence: Its strategy of premium brands and scale efficiency is well understood and widely copied.

trend.evidence: It does not benefit from a major platform shift; beer faces moderation headwinds.

dr1.evidence: Underlying EPS rose 23.4% in 2Q26 and 22.1% in HY26, it beat EPS consensus in each of the last six quarters, and consensus FY2026 EPS growth is about 18%.

dr2.evidence: Continued deleveraging, lower interest costs and buybacks should lift EPS, but much of this is already expected by analysts.

dr4.evidence: A weaker US dollar and lower interest rates help reported results and refinancing, but emerging-market currency swings remain a risk.

dr6.evidence: Q3 2026 results (around Oct 29), the ongoing $6B buyback ($4.1B left as of 24 July 2026) and further debt reduction are identifiable drivers.

dr7.evidence: With slow organic growth and high leverage, it is unlikely to justify a large concentrated position under Druckenmiller's approach.

gm.evidence: FY2025 gross margin was 55.9% ($33,179M of $59,320M), high for a beverage producer.

fcfyield.evidence: FY2025 free cash flow of $11,331M equals about 6.8% of a roughly $166B market value at $82.59, attractive for a dominant staple.

gb2.evidence: LTM profit from operations of about $16.6B is about 6.9% of an enterprise value near $240B (including net debt and minority interests), moderate rather than high.

pa2.evidence: The 2023 US Bud Light setback has largely been absorbed (it was the #1 share gainer in US total alcohol in HY26), but the long-run decline in beer volumes is structural.

pa4.evidence: Durable brands, $21.2B of normalized EBITDA and $11.3B of free cash flow make permanent loss of capital unlikely despite leverage.

wo1.evidence: It is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Beer production costs are not falling quickly with volume; volumes fell 2.3% in FY2025.

wo3.evidence: It combines no innovation platforms; its digital BEES app is an efficiency tool for a traditional business.

wo4.evidence: The global beer market grows slowly and will not be many times larger in five years.

ac3.evidence: It is exposed to aluminium and barley prices, emerging-market currencies and interest rates on about $72B of debt.

ns1.evidence: It uses scale to raise margins (EBITDA margin up 101bps to 35.8% in FY2025) and revenue per hectolitre (+4.4%) rather than pass savings to customers.

ns4.evidence: Lower debt and premium brands may strengthen it, but category headwinds make a clearly stronger position in 10-20 years uncertain.

va2.evidence: Beer is a discretionary pleasure, not a solution to a large, painful problem.

tn1.evidence: It sells into a mature beer category, not a secular growth trend.

tn2.evidence: The market sees it as a big brewer, which is what it is; BEES Marketplace is too small to change the story.

tn3.evidence: It is a large-cap, non-Chinese, non-commodity, non-seasonal established company.

tn4.evidence: It is profitable ($6,837M in FY2025) but revenue fell slightly in 2025 (-0.8% reported) and debt ($72.3B) far exceeds cash ($8.0B), so it passes only one of three cleanly.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow is positive over each half-year (HY26 $3,881M) but debt has exceeded cash in every quarter.

tn6.evidence: Organic revenue grew 2.0% in FY2025 and 5.7% in HY26 (reported FY2025 -0.8%).

tn7.evidence: FY2025 revenue growth (-0.8%) plus FCF margin (19.1%) is about 18, below 40.

tn8.evidence: In HY26 revenue grew 11.5% while profit from operations grew 15.8%, so revenue outpaced operating expenses; in FY2025 cost of sales fell 2.3% versus a 0.8% revenue decline.

tn9.evidence: It hits instant kills: debt ($72.3B) exceeds cash ($8.0B) and revenue growth is below 10%.

tn10.evidence: No existential legal threat is known, but alcohol faces rising excise taxes, health-warning rules and advertising restrictions worldwide.

tn11.evidence: It provides beer and other drinks that help retailers and bars serve adult consumers and make money, charging per unit sold, and customers pick it for famous brands and reliable supply.

tn13.evidence: Total about 60/130: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 0, operating margin 10 (about 26.5% LTM), short interest 10, institutional ownership 0 (ADS float mostly held by the reference shareholder structure), revenue vs expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 500 0, moat 10, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 0, culture/mission 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue fell in 2025, gross margin fell from 58.1% (2020) to 55.9% (2025) and debt exceeded cash every year, though free cash flow stayed positive.

tn15.evidence: Coverage is about 3.0x (profit from operations $15,405M ÷ finance expense $5,146M), assets excluding goodwill are 0.83x liabilities and the current ratio is 0.72; only liabilities/equity (1.24x) passes.

tn18.evidence: Doukeris has a strong execution record since 2021 but has been CEO only about five years, is not a founder and no notable open-market share purchases were found.

tn20.evidence: It beat EPS consensus in each of the last six quarters, including Q2 2026 ($1.21 vs $1.09).

tn21.evidence: There is no clown CEO, co-CEO, fraud suspicion or current acquisition spree, but gross margin has declined since 2020 and the company has a history of debt-fuelled mega-deals.

tn22.evidence: It has $59B of revenue, strong cash flow, buys back shares rather than issuing them and is not a hype stock.

tn24.evidence: At a 10% discount rate and its 17.6% FCF margin, the $82.59 price implies roughly 9% annual revenue growth, above the 0.9% three-year average and 2-6% organic growth it is delivering.

tn25.evidence: Nash's DCF (0.9% growth, 17.6% FCF margin, 4% terminal growth, net debt of $64.3B, 2,009M shares) gives about $27 per share at 12%, far below $82.59.

tn26.evidence: Forward P/E is about 19x (FY2026 EPS estimate $4.40), in line with large brewers, and MarketBeat's PEG is 1.19, above 1.
